mainEntity.name: Is it normal for gums to bleed when I brush around my dental implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Occasional minor bleeding when brushing around an implant may occur, particularly if plaque has accumulated or if you have recently changed your brushing technique. However, bleeding that happens consistently every time you brush is a sign that the tissue may be inflamed. This warrants a review of your oral hygiene technique and, if it persists, a professional assessment. It is never advisable to simply brush less vigorously to avoid bleeding — this often worsens the underlying cause.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if I have peri-implantitis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peri-implantitis cannot be self-diagnosed. It is identified during a clinical examination, where your dentist or hygienist will gently probe the tissue around the implant to assess pocket depths, check for bleeding on probing, and may take radiographs to evaluate the bone level. Common symptoms that prompt investigation include persistent bleeding, swelling, bad taste, or implant discomfort — but some cases are detected at routine check-ups before noticeable symptoms develop.

Peri-implantitis can be managed, although outcomes vary depending on how advanced the condition is at the time of diagnosis. Early-stage cases often respond well to professional cleaning and improved oral hygiene. More advanced cases may require surgical intervention to access and clean the implant surface and address bone loss. Treatment success depends on a range of individual factors, and suitability for specific approaches can only be determined following a thorough clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: Does bleeding around an implant mean the implant is failing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Bleeding around an implant most commonly reflects tissue inflammation (peri-implant mucositis) rather than implant failure. However, if bleeding is associated with other symptoms such as mobility, significant bone loss, or deep infection, these findings may have implications for the long-term prognosis of the implant. Only a clinical assessment — including examination and radiographic evaluation — can determine the health status of an implant and the options available.

mainEntity.name: How often should I have my dental implant checked?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most patients with dental implants are advised to attend a maintenance appointment at least every six months, though some individuals may be advised to attend more frequently based on their personal risk profile. These appointments typically include professional cleaning, tissue assessment, and monitoring of the peri-implant structures. Regular attendance allows any early changes to be identified and addressed promptly.

mainEntity.name: Can I use an electric toothbrush on my dental implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, electric toothbrushes — particularly oscillating-rotating or sonic models — can be safe and effective for cleaning around dental implants. Using a soft or extra-soft brush head and applying gentle pressure is advisable. Some patients find that electric brushes are more effective at disrupting plaque than manual brushing, which can be beneficial for implant health. If you are unsure about the most appropriate brush type for your situation, your dental team can provide personalised guidance.
